steps.tx: The **Denis three-column classification** of thoracolumbar spinal injuries was formulated by Francis Denis in 1983, replacing earlier two-column models to predict mechanical instability and neurological risk. Denis conceptualized the osteoligamentous spine into anterior, middle, and posterior functional columns. Establishing column integrity determines whether a fracture pattern will heal in an external orthosis or requires operative instrumented stabilization.
steps.say: Francis Denis introduced his three-column concept in 1983, revolutionizing spinal trauma assessment. By dividing the spinal column into anterior, middle, and posterior zones, this model predicts mechanical collapse and spinal cord injury, dictating whether surgery is needed to restore stability.

vis.title: Denis Three-Column Anatomical Boundaries
rows: ALL, anterior 2/3 vertebral body and disc
Pedicles, facets, laminae, spinous processes, PLC

steps.tx: The structural cornerstone of the model is the **middle column**, which comprises the posterior one-third of the vertebral body, posterior one-third of the intervertebral disc, and the posterior longitudinal ligament. Denis demonstrated that middle column integrity serves as the crucial biomechanical fulcrum. Disruption of two or more columns, or any structural failure involving the middle column, renders the spinal fracture unstable.
steps.say: The middle column is the key to spinal stability. It consists of the posterior third of the vertebral body, posterior disc, and posterior longitudinal ligament. If the middle column is disrupted, the spine is inherently unstable and vulnerable to progressive deformity or neurological damage.

right.title: Instability Determinants
points: Disruption of two or more columns

steps.tx: In a **compression fracture**, failure occurs under axial flexion loading confined strictly to the anterior column. The middle and posterior columns remain completely intact and stable. Radiographs demonstrate anterior wedging of the vertebral body with loss of anterior vertebral height, but the posterior cortical wall height is fully preserved, ruling out retropulsion of bone fragments into the neural canal.
steps.say: In a compression fracture, failure under flexion is restricted to the anterior column only. The middle and posterior columns stay completely intact. Anteroposterior and lateral X-rays show anterior wedging, but the posterior vertebral wall height is perfectly preserved, meaning zero danger of canal compromise.

vis.title: Compression versus Burst Fracture
rows: Failed in compression; posterior wall fractured
Present; bone fragments displaced into canal

steps.tx: A **burst fracture** results from high-energy axial loading that shatters both the anterior and middle columns simultaneously. Failure of the posterior vertebral body wall propels retropulsed bone fragments into the spinal canal, placing the conus medullaris and cauda equina roots at grave risk of compressive neuropathy. Computed tomography is indispensable to quantify the percentage of canal occlusion and facet joint diastasis.
steps.say: A burst fracture happens when massive axial force crushes both the anterior and middle columns together. The posterior vertebral wall shatters, driving retropulsed bone fragments directly into the spinal canal. Obtain an immediate computed tomography scan to measure canal narrowing and guide decompression.

left.title: Burst Fracture Pathomechanics
points: Simultaneous anterior and middle column failure
Axial load drives nucleus into vertebral body

right.title: Neurological Vulnerability
points: High risk of conus medullaris injury (T12-L1)
Cauda equina root compression below L2

steps.tx: The remaining major categories comprise flexion-distraction injuries (Chance fractures) and **fracture-dislocations**. Chance fractures represent seatbelt injuries where tension forces fail the posterior and middle columns while the anterior column acts as a hinge. Fracture-dislocations represent catastrophic three-column failure caused by shear, torsion, or distraction, carrying the highest incidence of permanent complete paraplegia and demanding urgent reduction and stabilization.
steps.say: Seatbelt or Chance fractures occur when the posterior and middle columns fail under tension while the anterior column hinges forward. Fracture-dislocations represent catastrophic failure across all three columns from violent shear or torsion, carrying the highest risk of complete, permanent paraplegia.

quiz.q: Which column is considered the critical biomechanical determinant of spinal stability in the Denis classification?
quiz.explain: The middle column (posterior 1/3 of vertebral body, disc, and PLL) is the crucial biomechanical fulcrum; its failure defines an inherently unstable spinal injury.

quiz.q: Which Denis fracture category features simultaneous failure of both the anterior and middle columns under axial compression with canal retropulsion?
quiz.explain: Burst fractures are characterized by axial compressive failure of both the anterior and middle columns, resulting in retropulsion of posterior vertebral body fragments into the spinal canal.
